L5@P0: Abstract
L6@P0: Multi-core neural processing units (NPUs) have emerged
L7@P0: to scale the computation capability of NPUs to e
L8@P0: ciently
L9@P0: support diverse machine learning tasks. In such multi-core
L10@P0: NPUs, workloads in di
L11@P0: erent cores can a
L12@P0: ect other co-runners
L13@P0: by incurring contentions on shared resources such as external
L14@P0: memory bandwidth and memory management unit (MMU)
L15@P0: for address translation. However, many recent NPU studies use
L16@P0: a single-core NPU framework without considering dynamic
L17@P0: e
L18@P0: ect by the shared resources. For this study, we develop a
L19@P0: new multi-core NPU simulator to assess the e
L20@P0: ect of resource
L21@P0: sharing accurately. Using the simulator, this paper reports
L22@P0: the sharing behaviors of multi-core NPUs with respect to
L23@P0: overall throughput and performance variance caused by corunners. The evaluation of the dual and quad core NPUs shows
L24@P0: that sharing MMU and memory bandwidth in general is
L25@P0: benecial for throughput, with minor degradation in fairness.
L26@P0: The evaluation also shows that page table walkers in MMU are
L27@P0: one of the critical shareable resources. Due to the bursty nature
L28@P0: of NPU memory accesses, sharing of walker bandwidth across
L29@P0: multiple cores can signicantly improve the performance.
L30@P0: The study extends the evaluation of scalability with multicore NPUs, investigating the e
L31@P0: ect of mapping heterogeneous
L32@P0: models to multiple NPUs.
L33@P0: 1. Introduction
L34@P0: Neural processing units (NPUs) have been increasing
L35@P0: their deployments from data centers to edge devices, partly
L36@P0: taking over the machine learning (ML) tasks from the
L37@P0: traditional GPUs. Such NPU architectures share a common
L38@P0: design with a systolic array for matrix multiplication and
L39@P0: software-managed on-chip scratch pad memory (SPM) for
L40@P0: staging data for the systolic array. To support a diverse
L41@P0: range of ML model sizes, a common approach is to have
L42@P0: multiple NPU cores in a single chip. Such multi-core NPUs
L43@P0: can avoid underutilization of a large single systolic array
L44@P0: when it processes small tasks. As big tasks can also be
L45@P0: 
L46@P0: exibly mapped to multiple cores by decomposition, multicore NPUs can adapt to a wide range of model sizes.
L47@P0: Such multi-core NPUs pose new challenges caused by
L48@P0: the interference on shared resources among cores. The
L49@P0: shared resources such as o
L50@P0: -chip memory bandwidth and
L51@P0: MMU (memory management unit) can potentially disrupt
L52@P0: the performance predictability of ML tasks on multi-core
L53@P0: *. Equal contribution.
L54@P0: NPUs as well as reducing overall throughput. The performance predictability is important to support service-level
L55@P0: objectives (SLO) on clouds, as many current SLO-supporting
L56@P0: schedulers assume that the latency of an inference task does
L57@P0: not change dynamically and rely on the proled latency for
L58@P0: SLO supports [7, 36, 39]. Contentions on shared resources
L59@P0: can dynamically change such latencies depending on corunners on di
L60@P0: erent cores in the same NPU.
L61@P0: However, most of the current NPU architecture studies
L62@P0: do not consider such resource sharing among NPU cores,
L63@P0: and thus the extents of potential benet and interference
L64@P0: have not been quantied. Such current simulation frameworks for NPUs can evaluate only a single core NPU
L65@P0: with a deterministic memory and MMU latency without
L66@P0: considering the runtime e
L67@P0: ects by memory bandwidth and
L68@P0: MMU sharing. However, NPUs often generate large bursts
L69@P0: of memory accesses from the on-chip scratchpad memory
L70@P0: (SPM), and they can saturate the MMU and memory
L71@P0: bandwidth, causing interference with co-runners. To address
L72@P0: the lack of evaluation on the sharing e
L73@P0: ects, we developed
L74@P0: a new multi-core NPU simulator, called mNPUsim, with a
L75@P0: detailed memory model using DRAMsim. The new multicore simulator can model dynamic memory latency changes
L76@P0: due to the contentions on the shared MMU and o
L77@P0: -chip
L78@P0: memory bandwidth.
L79@P0: Using the multi-core NPU simulator, this paper analyzes
L80@P0: the behavior of sharing MMU and memory bandwidth with
L81@P0: co-running ML workloads, for both of the performance and
L82@P0: fairness aspects. The rst observation from the analysis is
L83@P0: that resource sharing across NPUs on the same chip bring
L84@P0: signicant benets. Compared to an equal static partitioning
L85@P0: of resources across NPUs, sharing such resources improves
L86@P0: overall throughput, helped by the bursty nature of NPU
L87@P0: memory accesses. NPU accesses the MMU and o
L88@P0: -chip
L89@P0: memory in a bursty manner to ll the on-chip scratchpad
L90@P0: memory with double-bu
L91@P0: ering. Such behaviors allow NPUs
L92@P0: to utilize the resources more e
L93@P0: ciently by sharing than
L94@P0: by partitioning. Fairness for SLO support is degraded by
L95@P0: sharing, but the degradation is relatively minor.
L96@P0: Among the shared resources, sharing page table walkers
L97@P0: can bring the most benet. As shown by the prior work [16],
L98@P0: bursty memory accesses make the page table walker bandwidth critical for a single-core NPU. Sharing the page table
L99@P0: walkers multiplies the available page table walkers for a
L100@P0: core, as the bursts of memory accesses from di
L101@P0: erent NPUs
L102@P0: often do not occur simultaneously. We further investigate
L103@P0: whether various static partitioning schemes with di
L104@P0: erent

L135@P1: 2. Background
L136@P1: 2.1. Multi-Core NPU Architecture
L137@P1: Neural processing unit (NPU) is a dedicated processing unit for executing machine learning workloads. An
L138@P1: NPU includes computational units composed of multiple
L139@P1: processing engines (PEs) and interconnection between PEs
L140@P1: as well as the on-chip scratchpad memory (SPM) feeding
L141@P1: data to PEs. To increase the amount of data being fetched
L142@P1: from the SPM and forwarded to next PEs and to execute
L143@P1: more computation in a clock cycle, several prior work
L144@P1: have proposed NPU architectures with a large number of
L145@P1: computational units [17]. However, large NPU cores may
L146@P1: not be fully utilized due to characteristics of operations
L147@P1: or dimensions of tensors [17]. For example, in the systolic
L148@P1: array-based NPU architecture, a considerable proportion of
L149@P1: PEs are not properly utilized if a dimension of tensors are
L150@P1: smaller than the width or height of the systolic array.
L151@P1: To address the under-utilization problem of a big
L152@P1: monolithic NPU architecture, there has been increasing
L153@P1: interests in the multi-tenant DNN execution in NPU utilizing multiple relatively-small computational units [4, 5, 8,
L154@P1: 10, 26]. Multi-core NPU architectures can be more e
L155@P1: cient
L156@P1: than the monolithic NPU architecture as both small and
L157@P1: large workloads can utilize the resource (i.e., computation
L158@P1: unit, on-chip SPM, o
L159@P1: -chip memory bandwidth, etc.) of
L160@P1: small NPUs e
L161@P1: ciently.
L162@P1: Therefore, state-of-the-art NPU architectures such as
L163@P1: Google Cloud-TPU [11] and ARM Ethos-N77 [3] are organized with multiple moderate-size cores sharing some
L164@P1: resources. Figure 1 shows the general design of a multi-core
L165@P1: NPU system. Each core contains a private computation unit
L166@P1: (systolic array), a local SPM, and a private DMA engine
L167@P1: for DMA access between SPM and o
L168@P1: -chip memory. On
L169@P1: the other hand, memory-related resources including TLB,
L170@P1: page table walkers, and o
L171@P1: -chip memory are shared among
L172@P1: cores as displayed in blue in Figure 1.
L173@P1: 2.2. Shared Resource in Multi-Core Systems
L174@P1: The management of shared resources has been a key
L175@P1: issue in multi-core systems for making them run e
L176@P1: ciently
L177@P1: and fairly across multiple cores. The unbalanced distribution and monopolization of shared resources would cause
L178@P1: performance degradation and increase of tail latencies. On
L179@P1: the other hand, properly managing shared resources would
L180@P1: bring a signicant performance improvement compared
L181@P1: to the design with statically-partitioned resources. In this
L182@P1: study, we concentrate on three shared resources in multicore NPU systems: 1) o
L183@P1: -chip memory bandwidth, 2) page
L184@P1: table walker (PTW), and 3) translation lookaside bu
L185@P1: er
L186@P1: (TLB).
L187@P1: O
L188@P1: -chip memory bandwidth: In a multi-core system,
L189@P1: o
L190@P1: -chip memory bandwidth is partitioned or shared by
L191@P1: the memory controllers. While dedicating per-core bandwidth improves fairness by resource isolation, sharing the
L192@P1: entire bandwidth can bring performance improvement by a
L193@P1: higher utilization. With the pros and cons of sharing, the
L194@P1: dynamic contention of shared memory bandwidth should
L195@P1: be considered for modeling multi-core systems.
L196@P1: Memory management unit (MMU): In conventional
L197@P1: systems with NPU or GPU, IOMMU is shared among devices
L198@P1: in the same system [12, 40]. With the shared MMU, its page
L199@P1: table walkers (PTWs) and TLBs are shared among cores.
L200@P1: However, such a page-table walker bandwidth for handling
L201@P1: TLB misses is one of the key performance bottlenecks
L202@P1: in memory intensive workloads, and thus, sharing PTW
L203@P1: can potentially cause severe interference in co-runner
L204@P1: performance. The prior work, DWS [28], addresses the
L205@P1: shared PTW management for multi-tenant GPU systems.
L206@P1: The PTW contention from inter-GPU interleaving of PTW
L207@P1: accesses incurs a signicant performance degradation in
L208@P1: such systems. To reduce the degradation, DWS proposes a
L209@P1: dynamic PTW stealing technique to control the sharing of
L210@P1: PTW among GPUs.
L211@P1: Translation lookaside bu
L212@P1: er (TLB): To reduce TLB
L213@P1: misses, a multi-core system can share TLB capacity among
L214@P1: cores expecting hit rate improvement through expanded
L215@P1: TLB coverage, while TLB con
L216@P1: ict misses between cores
L217@P1: would cause performance interference among co-runners.
L218@P1: Least-TLB [21] proposed a contention-aware TLB design
L219@P1: for multi-GPU systems. Using separated TLBs as well as
L220@P1: a shared IOMMU TLB, Least-TLB improves the hit rate of
L221@P1: TLBs through spilling.
L222@P1: 2.3. Characteristics of NPU workloads
L223@P1: The prominent characteristic of workloads used in
L224@P1: NPUs is their regularity. Major operations in DNN models
L225@P1: such as convolution and general matrix-matrix multiplication (GEMM) operations can be naively represented in
L226@P1: the form of multi-level nested loops. Since nested loops
L227@P1: deterministically o
L228@P1: er data locality, there have been a
L229@P1: number of research about mapping operations into DNN
L230@P1: accelerators for e
L231@P1: ciently leveraging such data locality in
L232@P1: DNN models [6, 20, 27, 43]. Especially, tiling strategies
L233@P1: have been employed in accelerators because nested loops
L234@P1: of convolution and GEMM operations can be reordered
L235@P1: when there is no dependency except reduction [24, 32].
L236@P1: Partitioning of input data into smaller subsets can exploit
L237@P1: parallelism in spatial accelerators to reduce data tra
L238@P1: c [17].

L265@P2: Figure 2: Overlapping memory access and computation
L266@P2: Another interesting characteristic of NPU workloads is
L267@P2: bursty memory requests due to pipelining techniques used
L268@P2: in conventional NPUs such as double bu
L269@P2: ering [26]. The
L270@P2: double bu
L271@P2: ering technique divides SPM into two half-sized
L272@P2: SPMs, and allocates them for two consequent operations.
L273@P2: Figure 2 (a) illustrates an example of pipelining widely
L274@P2: used in conventional NPUs. When the tensor size is larger
L275@P2: than a half of SPM capacity, it can be split into multiple
L276@P2: tiles. With the tiling method, the memory access time and
L277@P2: computation time are overlapped to improve PE utilization
L278@P2: in NPUs.
L279@P2: Figure 2 (b) shows the moving average of memory
L280@P2: requests between SPM and o
L281@P2: -chip memory during 1000
L282@P2: cycles window when executing the NCF workload in a
L283@P2: single-core NPU conguration of our simulator, which
L284@P2: will be explained in Section 3 and Section 4.1 in detail.
L285@P2: As described in Figure 2 (b), memory requests occurring
L286@P2: when the tile read or write phase begins do not occur
L287@P2: constantly, but a large amount of accesses may occur in
L288@P2: a short period of time [12, 16]. Moreover, because of the
L289@P2: virtually-addressed SPM replacing physical cache, every
L290@P2: o
L291@P2: -chip memory request requires address translation. For
L292@P2: example, when the SPM size is tens of MB, thousands of
L293@P2: pages are included in one tile as the tile size is a half
L294@P2: of SPM size in common NPU architectures. Accordingly,
L295@P2: thousands of address translations are required to read and
L296@P2: write a tile in SPM. Moreover, reading or writing a tile
L297@P2: may require many memory transactions, because a tile is a
L298@P2: multi-dimensional tensor mapped in 1D o
L299@P2: -chip memory
L300@P2: address space [16].
L301@P2: The burstiness of address translation and memory access
L302@P2: requests varies across layers even within a single DNN
L303@P2: model. For example, in a convolution neural network, the
L304@P2: computational intensity and memory intensity of each
L305@P2: convolution layer can be di
L306@P2: erent depending on various
L307@P2: factors such as the size of the input feature map or the
L308@P2: number of channels. To handle the large burstiness of
L309@P2: memory-intensive layers, memory resources such as o
L310@P2: -chip
L311@P2: memory bandwidth and PTWs need to be fully utilized for a
L312@P2: relatively long duration. On the other hand, in computationintensive layers, memory resources might need to be fully
L313@P2: utilized only for short periods or be partially utilized to
L314@P2: handle relatively small burstiness. Similarly, the utilization
L315@P2: of the computational units in NPU can signicantly vary depending on the characteristics of layers. However, e
L316@P2: ciently
L317@P2: computing layers with di
L318@P2: erent characteristics on the same
L319@P2: architecture is a di
L320@P2: cult problem because various factors
L321@P2: such as the characteristics of workloads, conguration of
L322@P2: the architecture, and SLO support must be considered.
L323@P2: 3. Simulator Design
L324@P2: To model the dynamic contention of shared resources
L325@P2: accurately, we developed mNPUsim, a C++ based cycleaccurate multi-core NPU simulator. mNPUsim simulates
L326@P2: homogeneous and heterogeneous systems with multiple
L327@P2: systolic array-based NPU cores.
L328@P2: 3.1. Modeling Multi-core NPU System
L329@P2: As a multi-core NPU simulator, mNPUsim satises
L330@P2: two major requirements: 1) dynamic modeling of shared
L331@P2: resources with multiple levels of sharing and 2) supporting
L332@P2: various heterogeneous core congurations.
L333@P2: Resource sharing: As shown in Figure 1, there are three
L334@P2: major shareable resources in a multi-core NPU architecture:
L335@P2: 1) o
L336@P2: -chip memory bandwidth (DRAM bandwidth), 2) page
L337@P2: table walker (PTW), and 3) TLB. To simulate dynamic
L338@P2: changes in shared resource occupation, mNPUsim rst supports out-of-order access for shared resources considering
L339@P2: read-after-write dependency and execution delay. The nondeterministic delay of o
L340@P2: -chip memory access is modeled
L341@P2: by integrating DRAMsim3 [22]. Moreover, when modeling
L342@P2: resource sharing, mNPUsim considers restrictions other than
L343@P2: the total amount of resource such as TLB set index, DRAM
L344@P2: bank and channel interleaving. We will cover the details of
L345@P2: resource sharing in Section 4.
L346@P2: Heterogeneous NPU cores and clock domain: mNPUsim supports heterogeneous NPU cores with di
L347@P2: erent
L348@P2: per-core congurations. Di
L349@P2: erent clock frequencies in NPU
L350@P2: cores and DRAM incur asynchrony for requests between
L351@P2: NPU and shared resources. To handle this, mNPUsim denes
L352@P2: two types of clocks: 1) global clock running with DRAM
L353@P2: clock frequency and 2) local clocks for each NPU core
L354@P2: frequency. Shared resource access requests are synchronized
L355@P2: to the global clock, and access latency is translated into
L356@P2: the local clock if necessary.
L357@P2: Operation mapping strategy: Other than those, mNPUsim follows the conventions of general NPUs. For
L358@P2: example, as most operations in DNN models including
L359@P2: convolution layers and fully connected layers can be
L360@P2: expressed as GEMM operations, conventional systolic array
L361@P2: based NPUs are designed with a focus on GEMM [42, 44].
L362@P2: Therefore, we also consider GEMM-based systolic array
L363@P2: designs in mNPUsim, adapting the image-to-column (im2col)
L364@P2: algorithm that rearranges an image or a batch into a matrix,
L365@P2: transforming convolution operations into GEMM operations
L366@P2: to be suitable for the systolic array. Since im2col is for
L367@P2: preprocessing data for GEMM, we assume that im2col can

L395@P3: 3.2. Simulation Details
L396@P3: 3.2.1. Conguration. mNPUsim receives ve kinds of
L397@P3: conguration les as input: 1) network_config contains
L398@P3: DNN topology information, including the dimension and
L399@P3: type of each layer as well as the connection between
L400@P3: layers. 2) arch_config species the hardware conguration
L401@P3: for NPU computation resources such as size of systolic
L402@P3: array, tile size, and data
L403@P3: ow. 3) npumem_config denes
L404@P3: the additional NPU hardware conguration. It species the
L405@P3: memory-related component conguration such as TLB and
L406@P3: (PTW) congurations. 4) dram_config describes the shared
L407@P3: resource conguration including DRAMsim3 conguration
L408@P3: le path, DRAM capacity, and level of resource sharing
L409@P3: (details in Section 4). 5) misc_config summarizes the execution mode of NPU core such as execution initiation time,
L410@P3: number of iterations, and the shared partition options of
L411@P3: page table walkers. Note that mNPUsim requires N numbers
L412@P3: of network_config, arch_config, and npumem_config for
L413@P3: N-core NPU architecture as they are per-core conguration,
L414@P3: while only one dram_config and misc_config are needed
L415@P3: because DRAM is always shared by all NPUs in mNPUsim.
L416@P3: 3.2.2. Simulation steps and results. As shown in Figure 3, mNPUsim is composed of two parts: 1) SW request
L417@P3: generator (Software stack) and 2) HW simulator (Hardware
L418@P3: stack). The SW request generator rst parses arch_config
L419@P3: and network_config les. With the given information, the
L420@P3: SW request generator and pre-run step produce the list of
L421@P3: memory requests for every tile. Memory requests consist
L422@P3: of address, size, and type of memory requests. The HW
L423@P3: simulator then follows the SW request generator to simulate
L424@P3: the multi-core NPU architecture from three inputs (memory
L425@P3: requests, npumem_config, and dram_config). HW simulator
L426@P3: runs an execution-driven simulation with given inputs,
L427@P3: modeling constraints described in Section 3.1.
L428@P3: The output of mNPUsim contains three types of information: 1) execution cycles, 2) PE utilization, and 3)
L429@P3: request logs of shareable resources. mNPUsim provides
L430@P3: the layer-wise execution cycle of each workload in NPU
